newsitem.title: JAPAN: New law helps Japan PM in US military base dispute.
newsitem.headline: New law helps Japan PM in US military base dispute.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto succeeded in pushing legislation through parliament on Thursday that enables him to override opposition to extending contracts for land used for U.S. military bases on Okinawa.

The bill was passed into law by the Upper House with votes from both Hashimoto's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party). It passed the Lower House last week.
The law allows Hashimoto's government to temporarily extend leases on land after current contracts on 3,000 plots on U.S. military bases on Okinawa expire on May 14.
It will allow the government to avoid illegally occupying the plots owned by anti-bases activists on Okinawa, where 75 percent of U.S. installations in Japan are located.
A majority of landowners have already agreed to extend the contracts. Land for the bases is leased by the central government, not by the U.S. military.

The bill's passage means Hashimoto has cleared a key political hurdle ahead of his April 25 summit in Washington with U.S. President Bill Clinton, where security issues will be a major item on the agenda.

But it also revealed a crack in the parliamentary alliance among the LDP, the Social Democrats and the tiny Sakigake party, that has kept Hashimoto in power since January 1996. The left-leaning Social Democrats voted against the bill.
The dispute over the U.S. bases on Okinawa flared up in September 1995 following the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen.
"The schedule (for extending the leases) became tight after the very unfortunate incident two years ago," Hashimoto said of the rape case after parliament passed the law.
"This is a minimal revision of current laws that enable us to fulfil our obligations under the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty," he said.

Okinawa, a strategic island in the East China Sea some 1,600 km (1,000 miles) southwest of Tokyo, is home to about half of the 40,000 U.S. military personnel in Japan. It hosts the large Kadena U.S. Air Force base as well as the only U.S. Marine Corps unit stationed outside the United States.
The concentration of U.S. military bases on Okinawa is a legacy of the 1945 Battle of Okinawa and the post-World War Two U.S. military administration of the island until 1972.

Since the rape case, the Okinawan prefectural government has campaigned for the closure of all bases by 2015 and accused the central government of treating the prefecture unfairly. Okinawa is also the poorest of Japan's 47 prefectures.
"We regret this law," Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota said in a statement issued in Washington, where he was visiting.
"The law discriminates against the Okinawan people and violates the constitutional right to ownership of property."
